name: Carmine Red
lede: Carmine Red is the rosy red that Werner's color list gave as its characteristic red, named for the pigment carmine and handed down through Syme's English edition of 1821.

sections.title: A name from Werner's list
sections.body:
Carmine Red is a name from the age of mineral and flower catalogues [1]. Abraham Werner built his color vocabulary from pigments, such as ochre-yellow and carmine-red, and from familiar objects, such as sky-blue [1]. Patrick Syme published the list in English, and his 1814 edition of 108 colors includes Carmine-red [1].

In Syme's 1821 edition it is no. 91 among the reds, and Baty calls it the characteristic color of Werner [2]. Werner described it as lake red lightly mixed with arterial blood red [2]. His examples were the [[flower:raspberry|raspberry]], the cockscomb and the [[carnation]] among plants, and the oriental [[gem:ruby|ruby]] among minerals [2]. Syme's illustrations add the feathers of the red myzomela, a New Guinea honeyeater, the petals of a cockscomb drawn in 1737, and rubies photographed for a mineral atlas in 1912 [2].

sections.title: A red used to build other colors
sections.body:
In these lists carmine red is also an ingredient. Werner described his [[crimson]] red as carmine red nudged toward blue with a dash of indigo [3]. His purplish red, which he called columbine red, takes a touch of Berlin blue and a smaller share of indigo on the same base [3]. Veinous blood red darkens the base with brownish black [3].

Blue and purple recipes borrow it too. Azure blue is Berlin blue warmed by a little carmine red, and Scotch blue carries only a slight tinge of it [3]. For Syme a bluish purple needs roughly as much carmine as Berlin blue, and a campanula purple pairs ultramarine and carmine in equal measure [4]. The red works as a base in the system, not as one shade among many.

sections.title: Which carmine?
sections.body:
The pigment word behind the name is slippery. The Pigment Compendium says carmine was first applied to scale-insect lakes in general, and that by the seventeenth century it was understood to mean a lake made from cochineal [5]. The insect story is told in the article on [[carmine]].

But carmine was not always an insect. Field's carmine, also called madder carmine, is the richest and deepest kind of madder lake, in the writings of Field and of Salter [6]. A modern tube of permanent carmine may be a naphthol AS-D azo pigment, according to Mayer [7]. Gurney's list of historic or not recommended pigments names carmine red [8]. The color name outlived the recipe several times over.

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The swatch here, #CE536B, is our library's approximation of Werner's aged swatch for no. 91 [9]. It is a rosy red, lighter and pinker than the deep red of [[carmine]] itself [9]. The paint standard RAL 3002 is a good deal deeper, at about #A1232B on screen [9].

Another system agrees with the rosy reading: Ridgway's 1912 plate XXVI has a near-duplicate called Spinel Red, at 0.6 CIEDE2000 units [9]. Its nearest named neighbor is [[cerise]], 5.0 units away, and Maerz and Paul's Mayflower is close behind [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is a rare color in painting. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a screen color within six units of the swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only three works [10]. They are an Indian *Ganesha* of about 1890 at 20 per cent, Jawlensky's [[painting:nga-130842|Red Path, St. Prex]] of 1915 at 15 per cent, and Patrick Henry Bruce's *Peinture/Nature Morte* of 1924 at 12 per cent [10]. All three date from 1890 to 1924 [10].

That puts it among the rarer named colors, rarer than 75 per cent of them [10]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [10].

questions.q: True or false: carmine has always meant a dye made from insects.
Which mineral did Werner give as the stone example of Carmine Red?

openers: Werner's carmine red was a recipe: lake red with a little arterial blood red.
In Syme's color lists carmine red is a building block: it goes into crimson, purplish red and even blues and purples.
Carmine was not always an insect: Field's carmine was madder, and permanent carmine can be an azo pigment.
